motivation: In 1979 Tajima (with the late John Dawson) showed theoretically that an intense laser pulse drives a plasma wake whose electric fields exceed those of conventional accelerators by three orders of magnitude. This insight, rooted in nonlinear plasma wave theory, became reality through the experiments of Malka and Leemans and their teams, who produced quasi-monoenergetic electron beams (2004) and then multi-GeV beams in centimetre-scale plasmas, with controlled injection, staging and stability. Laser wakefield acceleration now powers compact femtosecond X-ray and gamma sources, drives free-electron-laser demonstrations, and opens access to strong-field QED studies such as radiation reaction and pair creation near the Schwinger limit. It is a clear case of theoretical plasma physics predicting a concrete, measurable effect that experiment then realised, transforming how we accelerate matter and generate radiation under extreme conditions.
